figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: uni-robot-agent: results and system overview. Top: shared tools, execution, and feedback connect models to environment adapters, supporting generalizable agentic training across environments. Bottom: Simulation and real-world scores.
figures.headline: Shared tools and feedback connect several models to environment adapters, with simulation and real-world scores summarized below.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Five logical layers of uni-robot-agent. Requests flow from agent runtimes through orchestration and shared tools to domain services and native backends. Context policies and concrete backends are replaceable components; arrows summarize logical interactions rather than individual network connections.
figures.headline: Five logical layers route each tool call from agent runtime through orchestration and tools to native robot backends.
citing_sentences: A tool call passes through five layers with explicit interfaces (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Tool reuse across environments. Shared tools avoid $N\times M$ implementations. $T$: tool; $A$: adapter; $E$: environment.
figures.headline: Shared tools serve N tools across M environment adapters instead of requiring N times M separate implementations.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Serial interaction and pipelining. Reasoning ($R$) overlaps sequential tools ($T$); $T_{2}$ queues while $T_{1}$ runs. Solid/dashed arrows show submissions/results; shading marks overlap. Timings are schematic.
figures.headline: Pipelining lets reasoning overlap sequential tools, with the second tool queued while the first is still running.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Key design choices. Each column pairs two designs for physical consistency, action precision, or context management.
figures.headline: Three columns each pair two design choices for physical consistency, action precision, or context management.
citing_sentences: We bind images, camera calibration, and robot state to an immutable snapshot and use that snapshot for localization (Figure 5).
We record request identities and execution status to reject duplicates (Figure 5).
Our move tool accepts a target pose and an optional gripper opening together, allowing the arm and gripper to act simultaneously (Figure 5).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Robot-use performance across model generations, families, and sizes. Success rate (top) and Score (bottom) on RoboDojo with uni-robot-agent. Robot use is neither exclusive to frontier models nor unique to the latest generation: GPT-5.6 Sol already achieves nontrivial performance, while Qwen3.8-27B succeeds where larger, earlier Qwen models fail. Shading indicates closed-source models.
figures.headline: GPT-5.6 Sol reaches 19.17% success and 24.04 Score, while Qwen3.8-27B succeeds where larger earlier Qwen models fail.
citing_sentences: Figure 6 shows that GPT-5.6 Sol already achieves a nontrivial 19.17% SR and 24.04 Score, while GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 37.50% SR and 45.63 Score.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Four capabilities associated with effective robot use. Correlation between each model’s RoboDojo Score and its errors in (a) general visual understanding, (b) spatial grounding, (c) coding in geometry, and (d) embodied reasoning. Lower error rates across these dimensions are associated with higher task performance, suggesting that effective robot use draws on a combination of these capabilities
figures.headline: Lower error rates in the four failure types are associated with higher RoboDojo Score across the evaluated models.
citing_sentences: Figure 7 summarizes these four failure types across thirteen models.

GPT-6.1 Sol achieves the lowest spatial-grounding failure rate among the evaluated models (31.5%), but this substantial remaining error rate highlights precise spatial grounding as a common challenge for further improvement (Figure 7b).
The pattern suggests that reliable robot-specific computation is another capability associated with effective robot use (Figure 7c).

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Robot-use performance and general model capabilities. Each point denotes a model, with benchmark performance on the horizontal axis and RoboDojo Score on the vertical axis. Q35–Q38 denote Qwen Flash generations; DS denotes DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017. Dashed lines show linear fits; Pearson correlations are computed across the six models.
figures.headline: Scores on four general benchmarks correlate with RoboDojo Score, most strongly for embodied reasoning and visual understanding.
citing_sentences: To investigate this, we compare RoboDojo performance with scores on four corresponding benchmarks: MMMU-Pro (Yue et al., 2024) for general visual understanding, ERQA (Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025) for embodied reasoning, ScreenSpot-Pro (Li et al., 2025) for spatial grounding, and LiveCodeBench v6 (Jain et al., 2024) for code generation (Figure 8).

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Robot use with less geometric information. Recorded progress through 771 tool calls and final score across 42 tasks, with skills enabled.
figures.headline: Depth removal costs Qwen less than removing camera parameters, which lowers its score to 9.13.
citing_sentences: Evidently, Astra’s score changes from 55.83 to 55.04, and Qwen’s score changes from 35.89 to 31.39, retaining 98.6% and 87.5% of their depth-enabled scores, respectively (Figures 9 and 9), reflecting a minimal loss in performance, especially with stronger model capabilities.

Without camera parameters (only RGB images), where agents must infer 3D positions from abstract spatial relationships, Qwen’s performance shows a sharp drop to 9.13, while Astra shows a moderate decrease on its performance to 31.29 (Figure 9).

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Effect of skill guidance on task performance. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with uni-robot-agent, evaluated with and without skills. Error bars indicate approximate 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
figures.headline: Skill guidance changes Qwen's aggregate score only slightly, with bootstrap confidence intervals shown as error bars.
citing_sentences: Figure 10 shows a small aggregate performance gap between configurations with and without robot skills.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Model-level resource–performance trade-offs. Astra, Qwen, and DeepSeek each use 252 episodes. Bars show score and mean resource usage per episode.
figures.headline: Qwen reaches 31.39 Score at 1.09 USD per episode, while GPT-6 Astra reaches 51.90 at 21.29 USD.
citing_sentences: Figure 11 shows that Qwen offers a favorable trade-off between the performance and the cost, reaching 31.39 score at \$1.09 per episode.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: Task progress over token usage and time. score is aggregated from recorded intermediate outcomes for the same model cohorts as Figure 11. Curves retain each episode’s latest observed score.
figures.headline: Astra reaches a score of 25 with 7.4M tokens, against 23.5M for Qwen and 49.9M for DeepSeek.
citing_sentences: Figure 12 shows that each models need substantially different amount of tokens to make progress.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Model–action overlap in pipelined execution. Blue and green bars show model requests and physical actions; shading marks overlap. Percentages indicate the fraction of action time overlapping model requests. Each panel starts at the first action and uses its own time range.
figures.headline: Pipelined episodes overlap 84.5% to 93.8% of physical execution with model requests, while serial episodes overlap none.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 13, it ranges from 84.5% to 93.8% in the pipelined episodes and is zero in all five serial episodes, showing that most of the physical execution time is pipelined with the model inference.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Episode duration on five selected tasks. Pipelined and serial execution are compared using one episode per configuration and task, excluding simulator initialization.
figures.headline: Pipelining shortens episode duration on all five tasks, with reductions ranging from 4.8% to 73.7%.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 14, the pipelined runs have shorter episode durations on all five tasks, with observed reductions ranging from 4.8% to 73.7% relative to serial execution.

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Agent-written triangulation in insert_tubes. Matching pixels marked A define viewing rays, illustrated schematically above the executed code excerpt. Recorded coordinates and reprojection errors connect the calculation to its output; the final frame follows subsequent grasping and insertion.
figures.headline: Agent-written triangulation places a tube cap within 0.46 and 1.94 pixels of the selected points in two views.
citing_sentences: Figure 15 follows one cap: the calculated position reprojects within 0.46 and 1.94 pixels of the selected points in the two views.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: Geometric hypothesis testing in cover_blocks. The agent varies a candidate table height and computes cup dimensions from selected pixels. The schematic illustrates the ray–plane intersections computed by hit() in the code excerpt; the right-hand frame shows a later placement over the red block.
figures.headline: The agent varies a candidate table height and compares resulting cup dimensions to test its scene geometry.
citing_sentences: The agent extracts colored image regions and writes code that tests candidate table heights, intersects pixel rays with each candidate plane, and compares the resulting cup dimensions (Figure 16).

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: Grasp adjustment and supported sliding in align_blocks. The upper row summarizes four stages, each illustrated by a representative observation; a stage may contain multiple tool calls. Green and blue bars show physical tools and model requests; shading marks overlap. The marked interval is enlarged below, where the model prepares a clearance check during release. Image timestamps and the main axis are relative to the first displayed observation.
figures.headline: The agent prepares a clearance check during gripper release, then switches to supported sliding after a lift fails to retain the square.
citing_sentences: Figure 17 follows the trajectory from an uncertain grasp through contact adjustments to the final aligned row.

figures.label: Figure 18
figures.caption: Orientation preparation during digit transport. The upper row summarizes four stages rather than individual tool calls; the lanes below show recorded execution. The enlarged interval shows a model request preparing rotation candidates while transport continues. The later divergence is retained to show how execution feedback affects the prepared plan. Colors and time conventions match Figure 17.
figures.headline: The agent prepares rotation candidates during transport, and later divergence shows that execution feedback can change the plan.
citing_sentences: The excerpt in Figure 18 follows one digit from localization and grasping through transport and reorientation.

abstract: Robot-use agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training. To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra–RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.

sections.body: Frontier robot-use agents are proprietary, so their weights cannot be trained. The paper introduces `uni-robot-agent`, a unified harness with shared tools, efficient execution, and modular runtimes. Without privileged inputs, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next reaches a Score of 31.39 on RoboDojo, above the 28.97 reported for GPT-6 Astra with RoboProbe. On 19 real-world tasks it scores 49.50, against 35.50 for Dream-1 and 47.75 for fine-tuned π0.5. The authors then compare models across generations, families, and sizes, and identify four capabilities (visual understanding, spatial grounding, geometric coding, and embodied reasoning) as targets for future training.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Proprietary models block robot-use training, so this paper offers an open, trainable harness that reaches competitive scores.

sections.body: The harness follows four principles: unified, efficient, realistic, and modular. Shared tools use common arguments, units, and feedback formats, and environment adapters translate them into native commands. Efficiency comes from background tool calls and resource-aware scheduling, so reasoning overlaps physical execution. Realistic operation excludes simulator depth and task-verifier feedback. The design choices include an immutable snapshot that binds images, calibration, and robot state, rejection of duplicate requests after communication failures, a move tool that checks progress at each step, and a `flush_queue` call that cancels calls that have not started. A sliding window replaces old images with text placeholders. This section describes the design and gives no quantitative evaluation of these choices.
sections.heading: uni-robot-agent: A Unified and Modular Harness
sections.headline: Shared tools, five logical layers, and six design choices let agents run without simulator depth or verifier feedback.

sections.body: On RoboDojo's 42 tasks, averaged over three seeds and two layouts (252 episodes), Qwen3.8-Flash-Next with uni-robot-agent reaches a 25.00% success rate and a Score of 31.39. This is above the listed VLA and WAM baselines and above GPT-6 Astra with RoboProbe, which reaches 22.48% and 28.97. Replacing the harness with GAP (Hybrid) lowers the same model by 8.89% in success rate and 10.38 Score. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reaches 21.39% and 27.11. In the real-world evaluation on 19 tasks, Qwen scores 49.50, close to fine-tuned π0.5 at 47.75 and above zero-shot Dream-1 at 35.50. The Qwen agent also receives depth from RealSense cameras, which the baselines do not use. Its precision score is 2.08/10.21, which is low.
sections.heading: Can Open Models Use Robots in Simulation and the Real World?
sections.headline: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next reaches 31.39 Score on RoboDojo and 49.50 on 19 real-world tasks.

sections.body: This section compares earlier generations, model families, and sizes. The added models were evaluated with one seed and one layout. GPT-5.6 Sol reaches a 19.17% success rate and 24.04 Score, and GPT-6.1 Sol reaches 37.50% and 45.63. Among Qwen models, success appears only from the 3.8 generation: Qwen3.8-27B reaches 8.06%, while Qwen3.5-122B and other earlier Qwen models record zero. Trajectory analysis identifies four failure types: visual understanding, spatial grounding, geometry coding, and embodied reasoning. Error rates for these types are associated with Score across 13 models. Benchmark scores for MMMU-Pro, ERQA, ScreenSpot-Pro, and LiveCodeBench v6 correlate positively with Score across six models, with spatial grounding showing the weakest correlation.
sections.heading: What Capabilities Enable Robot-Use Agents?
sections.headline: Robot use appears across model generations and families, and four failure types suggest joint training targets.

sections.body: Two ablations test whether privileged information drives performance. For depth (RQ1), GPT-6 Astra changes from 55.83 to 55.04 without depth but with camera parameters, retaining 98.6% of its depth-enabled score. Qwen changes from 35.89 to 31.39, retaining 87.5%. Without camera parameters as well, Qwen drops to 9.13 and Astra reaches 31.29. For skills (RQ2), disabling the Qwen skill library gives 30.31 Score and a 24.58% success rate, a gap of 0.42 percentage points in success rate. The authors conclude that depth is not necessary when camera parameters are available, and that the skill library is not needed for comparable performance. GPT-6 Astra used one seed and one layout because of evaluation cost.
sections.heading: Analysis on Privileged Information
sections.headline: Removing camera parameters drops Qwen to 9.13, while removing skills changes Score from 31.39 to 30.31.

sections.body: This section reports cost, token use, wall-clock time, and the effect of pipelining. Qwen reaches 31.39 Score at 1.09 USD per episode, while GPT-6 Astra reaches 51.90 at 21.29 USD. To reach a score of 25, Astra needs 7.4M tokens per episode, against 23.5M for Qwen and 49.9M for DeepSeek. In wall-clock time, Astra reaches a score of 25 after 42.6 minutes, against 95.5 and 99.2 minutes for Qwen and DeepSeek. On five tasks run with Astra at medium reasoning effort, pipelined runs are shorter on every task, with reductions from 4.8% to 73.7%. The fraction of physical execution overlapping model requests ranges from 84.5% to 93.8% in pipelined episodes, and is zero in serial episodes. Each configuration was run once per task.
sections.heading: Analysis on Cost and Speed
sections.headline: Qwen costs 1.09 USD per episode for 31.39 Score, and pipelining cuts episode time on all five tested tasks.

sections.body: Vision-language-action models transfer pretrained visual-language representations to robot control, and π0.5 combines robot experience with web data. World-action models such as DreamZero and Cosmos Policy predict future states or jointly generate video and actions. Tool-using agents appear in computer-use settings and, in robotics, through skill selection and programmatic composition of control APIs. Recent robot-use harnesses include RoboDawn, Robo-Harness K1, OpenRUA, Harness VLA, GAP, and ORA, each offering different tools, memory, or correction mechanisms. The authors note that reliable use of past observations and recovery from failures remain open problems. uni-robot-agent separates shared robot tools from model runtimes and environment adapters, and coordinates tool execution so that reasoning continues during motion.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior robot-use harnesses offer varied tools and interfaces, so this work separates shared tools from model runtimes.

sections.body: The paper presents uni-robot-agent as a unified, modular harness for robot-use agents. Its evaluations include GPT-6 Astra in simulation and the real world. They show that Qwen3.8-Flash-Next reaches a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, above the 28.97 for Astra with RoboProbe. The authors argue that open-weight models that can run locally and be adapted through training on robot experience merit further study. Precise manipulation and reliable long-horizon execution remain challenges in their evaluations. Shared interaction interfaces, replaceable components, and structured execution feedback are offered as a base for collecting interaction data, developing training methods, and measuring their effects.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: An open-weight model with the harness reaches 31.39 Score, while precise manipulation and long-horizon execution remain open.

sections.body: The appendix lists simulation baselines and reasoning effort settings, and describes the Real Eval hardware, baselines, and 19-entry test catalogue across five dimensions. It gives the scoring formula, which awards partial credit for individual criteria, and per-task results behind Table 2. The training catalogue contains 30 task templates and 1,550 trajectories, and is used only to fine-tune π0.5, not uni-robot-agent. Appendix E presents agent-written geometry code in `insert_tubes` and `cover_blocks`. Appendix F presents two trajectories in `align_blocks` and `arrange_largest_number` that show planning during physical execution.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists baselines, real-world task catalogue and scoring rules, per-task results, and agent case studies.
